title: May all be well
hookLine: a medal goes in a drawer; Shantideva finishes his poem and gives its good away to every being
tomorrow: who are the first people on Shantideva's list of wishes?

lines: THE MEDAL GOES IN A DRAWER.
cards: After the charity run, the medal goes in a drawer. After the big project, the file gets saved, and maybe somebody says thanks in a meeting. Shantideva finishes his poem and does something else with what it earned.
He gives it away. The last chapter opens with a wish: by whatever good came from writing this, may all beings enter the way of awakening. And then, verse after verse, he names exactly who he means.

teach.b: This is dedicating merit. In Sanskrit, parinamana: turning over, turning the good of an act toward others. Buddhist chanting and study can end this way, with the good handed on.
And inside the tradition, people have argued about it. One side quotes the Dhammapada: by oneself evil is done, and by oneself one is made pure; no one purifies another.

teach.h: ONE SIDE: KARMA IS YOUR OWN.
teach.b: Karma is your own. So how could anyone hand it over, like a gift card? That's a real point, and it protects something: nobody can do your practice for you.

teach.h: OTHER SIDE: GIVING IS ITSELF GOOD.
teach.b: The other side points to the practice itself. In Theravada tradition, families share merit with relatives who have died, and an old sutta describes the departed rejoicing at gifts given in their name.

Mahayana texts like Shantideva's dedicate merit to all beings, with no limit at all. Their best case goes like this: nothing is being moved from one account to another. The giving away is itself a good act.

A mind that opens its hands at the end of the work is changed by opening them. Some teachers hold both sides at once: your karma is yours, and wishing its good to everyone is a fine thing to do with it.
Shantideva doesn't stop to settle the argument.
He just gives it away, to every being he can name.

how: Buddhists in different schools close a practice, a chanting session or a day of study by dedicating its merit; in Theravada communities merit is also shared with relatives who have died, and in the Mahayana with all beings.

games.q: what does “may all be well” mean?
o: giving away the good of your practice to all beings
a toast wishing your friends good health and luck
a blessing a teacher gives students at the end of class

games.q: the debate, side by side — tap the pairs.
p: turning the good over to others
giving it away is itself good

s: dedicating merit is a Mahayana-only practice
Theravada families share merit with relatives who have died, too.
the Dhammapada says no one purifies another
that line is the heart of the case that karma is your own.
dedicating the good means you lose the good you did
on the sharing side's view, giving it away is itself a good act.

games.q: your friend says: "sharing merit makes no sense. karma is yours alone." what's the best case for dedicating anyway?
o: nothing gets moved like money; the giving away is itself a good act.
karma is only a metaphor, so it can go wherever you want it to.
you're right; dedicating is a nice ritual that does nothing.
games.why: both sides are inside the tradition. the Dhammapada protects 'your practice is yours'; the sharing side says opening your hands is itself the practice.

practice: Rest your hands open on your knees, palms up.

Bring this lesson to mind, the reading and the few minutes it took, and in the spirit of Shantideva's last chapter, wish whatever good it did to go everywhere: to people you know, and people you'll never meet.
Keep the hands open; there's nothing to hold.

wordCard.voice: May all be well: the dedication that ends Shantideva's poem, giving away whatever good it did to all beings.

orig.note: Sanskrit: dedication, turning over the good of an act toward the benefit of others.

carryVoice: For the road: for all, open hands at the end of the work. Forty-six down, four to go.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 10.1 (by the good of composing this, may all beings enter the bodhisattva's way)
Dhammapada 165 (by oneself evil is done; no one purifies another)
Khuddakapatha 7, Tirokudda Sutta (the departed rejoice at gifts given in their name)
